patent: Filed January 26, 1932 and issued February 20, 1934 to Ernest O. Lawrence of Berkeley, Calif., assigned to Research Corporation: the cyclotron patent, although the word cyclotron does not appear in it. Lawrence started from Wideröe's resonance linear accelerator (R. Wideröe, Archiv für Elektrotechnik 21, 387, 1928; cited in the patent), which needs ever longer drift tubes, and bent the ion path into a spiral with a uniform magnetic field so that one pair of electrodes gives every kick. The working point is that the revolution frequency qB/(2πm) (the patent's Equation (6)) does not depend on radius or speed, so a fixed-frequency oscillator stays in step while the ions gain energy; this holds only while the ion speed is well below c. The first reports were E. O. Lawrence and N. E. Edlefsen, Science 72, 376 (1930), and E. O. Lawrence and M. S. Livingston, Physical Review 40, 19 (1932). Figs. 1-2 give the principle and the electric and magnetic focusing, Figs. 3-5 a working machine with one insulated electrode against a grounded electrode and its circuits, Figs. 6-7 measured collector currents. Lawrence received the 1939 Nobel Prize in Physics for the invention and development of the cyclotron.

figs.1: View along the magnetic field, which is perpendicular to the page. Hollow half-cylinders 1 and 2 face each other across the diametral gap; the marks ∓ and ± show that their polarities are always opposite and alternate. The dashed and dash-dot arcs are one ion path: half circles of growing radius inside each electrode, joined across the gap, starting near the centre (arrow) and leaving at lower left as High Speed Ions. Oscillator 4 is wired across the two electrodes.
figs.2: Cut across the gap, perpendicular to the plane of Fig. 1: the radial direction runs up and down, the magnetic field left to right between the pole faces (3 on the left). Electrode 1 is at top and 2 at bottom, both drawn hatched; the thin line a—a is the central plane seen edge-on. Dash lines m are magnetic lines of force, straight in the middle and bowed near the top and bottom edges of the poles; the heavy arrows at top mark the resulting push toward the central plane. Dotted lines e bulge into each electrode mouth, and the dot and dash path p of an ion off the central plane is pulled toward it each time it crosses the gap.
figs.3: Outside of the machine, seen from the same side as Fig. 4. The slim box 8 with insulator 14 on top sits in the gap of magnet 11 between pole pieces 9 and 10. The two large blocks left and right are not numbered or described in the text.
figs.4: Cut through the casing and pole pieces, field running left to right. Upper electrode 6 is a hollow box open downward, held only by rod 12, which leaves the casing through a tube at the top; the two small hatched squares below its mouth are the grounded bars 7. Filament 30 in housing 57 sits beside the gap at left. In the lower half are walls 42 of electrode 40, with strip 41 below. Line 5—5 runs down the middle between the side walls, so Fig. 5 is the view in the plane where the ions circulate.
figs.5: The machine in its median plane plus the full wiring. Ions start at filament 30 between electrode 6 (upper half circle, its wall 13 dashed) and bars 7 (horizontal strip across the middle), spiral inside the dashed outline 10 of the pole faces, and at lower left run along channel 47 between 40 and 41 from inlet 49 to outlet 50, through iron channel 52' into collector box 51, or with 51 removed out through window 55. Circuits: oscillator 18 at top drives rod 12 (wire 22) against the casing (wire 23), powered by rectifier 20 from line 24; filament supply 31-35 and 200 V bias 36 at right; magnet current 26-29 at lower right; deflector supply 43-46 from a 1000 V source at bottom; collector current to electrometer 53 with its shunt at bottom left.
figs.6: Collector current against deflecting field between 40 and 41, oscillator wave length 37.5 m (about 8.0 MHz). The dashed triangles are the two measured peaks: protons (H^{+}) at 5250 gauss peaking near 1700 V/cm, and H_{2}^{+} at 10,500 gauss peaking near 3400 V/cm, twice the energy needing twice the field. Arithmetic on the text: Equation (9) with the printed r = 4.50 cm gives about 27,000 volts for protons at 5250 gauss; the stated 175,000 volts corresponds to r of about 11.4 cm, which is 4.50 inches.
figs.7: Collector current against magnet field with the deflecting field held at about 2500 V/cm. Current appears only in two narrow lines, at 5250 gauss (protons) and 10,500 gauss (H_{2}^{+}), the fields at which each ion's revolution matches the 37.5 m oscillation.

parts.7: In Figs. 3-5 the second electrode is not a hollow half-cylinder but a pair of grounded bars; the text notes that a second insulated hollow electrode, as in Figs. 1-2, would double the energy.
parts.10: In Fig. 5 numeral 10 marks the dashed circle showing the outline of the pole face behind the section.
parts.52: A soft-iron channel that shields the exit path from the magnetic field so the ions run outward on their own momentum.
parts.a: Printed a—a; the plane midway between the side walls of the electrodes, in which the ions circulate.

glossary.def: Later name for this machine; the patent calls it apparatus for the multiple acceleration of ions.
Later name for the hollow half-cylinder electrodes (1, 2, 6), after their D shape.
Here: the time of half a revolution in the magnetic field equals half the period of the electrode voltage, so each gap crossing meets an accelerating field.
f = qB/(2πm) in SI units; the patent's Equation (6) f = He/(2πcm) is the same in Gaussian units. Independent of radius and speed while the speed is well below c.
Proton; hydrogen molecular ion (two protons, one electron), with half the charge-to-mass ratio of the proton, so it resonates at twice the magnetic field.
CGS unit of magnetic flux density; 10,000 gauss = 1 tesla, so 10,500 gauss = 1.05 T.
Radio frequency quoted as free-space wavelength; f = c/λ, so 37.5 m is about 8.0 MHz.
Energy given as the single voltage step that would produce it; for a singly charged ion 175,000 volts means 175 keV.
Instrument for very small charges or currents; here measuring the collector current through a high resistance shunt, in units of 10^{-9} A.
Voltmeter that reads voltage from the attraction between charged plates and draws practically no current.
Here an adjustable voltage divider across the 1000 V source, setting the deflector voltage.
Vacuum tube with a heated cathode; in the oscillator it sustains the radio-frequency oscillation, in the energizing circuit it rectifies the alternating supply.
Forces that pull ions back toward the central plane: the electric field bulging into the electrode mouths and the outward-bowed magnetic field near the pole edges (Fig. 2).
